column1: # OWASP ZAP baseline — per-rule dispositions. TAB-separated: <rule id> <IGNORE|WARN|FAIL> <comment>
# THIS FILE IS THE ONLY PLACE A FINDING IS TOLERATED, and that is deliberate. `ci.yml` sets
# `fail_action: true`, so the job goes red on anything the scan reports — which means every accepted
# finding has to be written down here, with its rule id and a reason, where it shows up in a diff.
# The alternative the action offers by default (`fail_action: false`) is a scan that reports findings
# and exits 0: the same defect as the Sonar step that submitted an analysis and never read the
# verdict, and as the deleted stage 6.
# IGNORE means "this does not apply to this system", never "we could not be bothered". If a rule
# genuinely applies, fix it in `docker/traefik/dynamic.yml` — headers belong on the terminator —
# rather than adding a line here.
# NOTE: that run predates the move to the privileged pair, and this block asked for a run at 443 to
# replace it. THAT RUN EXISTS NOW -- `31301914764`, the first on the pinned engine, at 443:
#   FAIL-NEW: 0   WARN-NEW: 0   IGNORE: 2   PASS: 65
# The superseded tally is kept below for comparison because the DIFFERENCE is the informative part.
# It read `WARN-NEW: 1, PASS: 66`; one rule moved out of PASS and into IGNORE, and it is 10035.
# v3.49 removed HSTS for real, so the rule that used to PASS -- meaning the header was PRESENT --
# now fires and is dispositioned below. `PASS: Strict-Transport-Security` appears 0 times in the new
# log and appeared in every run before the fix.
# A tally measures a configuration, not the tool. Pinning the image changed none of it.
#   superseded, run 31257068048 at :8443 -- FAIL-NEW: 0   WARN-NEW: 1   PASS: 66
# At that run the TLS work's headers all passed on their own merits and needed no entry:
# Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Content Security Policy,
# Permissions Policy, Cross-Domain Misconfiguration, Private IP Disclosure and Application Error
# Disclosure.
# STRICT-TRANSPORT-SECURITY HAS SINCE BEEN TURNED OFF DELIBERATELY, so rule 10035 is expected to
# report it missing from the next run onward and is dispositioned below. That is a real reduction in
# what this gate asserts, and it is written down rather than absorbed.
# ── A LIMIT OF THIS SCAN, STATED RATHER THAN LEFT TO BE DISCOVERED ──────────────────────────────
# The same run reported:
#   Job spider error accessing URL https://127.0.0.1:8443 status code returned : 401 expected 200
# That is correct behaviour and it is also the ceiling on what this gate can see. A baseline scan
# spiders for links and then reads passively; this is a bearer-token JSON API with no anonymous
# surface and no hyperlinks, so the spider found exactly two URLs and both answered 401. **This job
# checks the edge — TLS, redirect, headers, error shapes — and does NOT scan the API's routes.**
# Adding authentication to *this* baseline would not help: with or without a token the spider still
# has no links to follow. That is why the ceiling is structural rather than a configuration miss.
# ── THE UPGRADE IS NOW WIRED, AND THESE TWO LINES USED TO DENY IT ───────────────────────────────
# They read: "The upgrade is `zap-api-scan.py` fed `docs/api/openapi.yaml` … It is not wired, and
# would need a token minted for it." Both halves became false the moment stage 11e landed, and this
# file went on asserting them — a stale claim introduced by the very change that closed the gap.
# Corrected here rather than in a follow-up, because the file that records a limit is the first
# place a reader checks whether it still applies.
# **Stage 11e wires exactly that**, in this same `zap` job, after this scan: `zap-api-scan.py -S`
# over the contract, with a token minted from Keycloak and proven live before ZAP is handed it.
# Measured on the same stack in the same run — 14 URLs against this scan's 3, 119 passive rules
# against its 66. Its dispositions live in `.zap/api-rules.tsv`, deliberately NOT here: that file
# dispositions the ROUTES, read with a credential; this one dispositions the EDGE, read without.
# The count above is also restated: at the current target (443, not the 8443 this file was written
# against) the baseline reaches `Total of 3 URLs`, not two.

column3: Non-Storable Content, on two 401 responses. The rule flags content a cache cannot store, which is a caching observation rather than a weakness — and on an authenticated ledger API non-storable is the REQUIRED behaviour, not a defect. Making this rule pass would mean making 401s cacheable.

Strict-Transport-Security Header Not Set. THIS ENTRY RESTED ON A FALSE PREMISE UNTIL THE APPLICATION WAS ACTUALLY CHANGED, and the correction is worth reading before trusting any other line here. The header was described as deliberately not sent, in this file and four documents, while the application SENT IT -- Traefik never configured it, but SecurityConfig carried no headers configuration at all, so Spring Security's default HstsHeaderWriter applied, and server.forward-headers-strategy=native makes RemoteIpValve mark proxied requests secure, which is the writer's only condition. The evidence was in this scanner's own output and went unread: rule 10035 reported PASS in both stage 11c and stage 11e, and a rule dispositioned IGNORE that had actually fired would have appeared in the IGNORE bucket instead (the baseline reported IGNORE: 1, which is 10049, and 11e's rules file carries no dispositions at all and reported WARN-NEW: 0). So this line was armed to silence the one alarm that could have reported the defect. SecurityConfig#hstsOff() now disables it on all three chains and SecurityConfigTest#hstsIsNotSentOnASecureRequest is the gate -- red proof measured, "Response should not contain header Strict-Transport-Security". The entry STAYS, because the header is now genuinely absent and the rule will genuinely fire; it is the one entry here that tolerates a real weakness rather than a non-applicable rule. The application's router is a catch-all, so a browser dialling https://localhost would receive the pin -- and HSTS is host-scoped and PORT-INDEPENDENT, so a one-year pin on the bare host `localhost` force-upgrades http://localhost:3000, http://localhost:8080 and every other local development server on that machine, failing with ERR_SSL_PROTOCOL_ERROR and clearable only through chrome://net-internals/#hsts. Breaking a developer's unrelated projects is too high a price for a header on a throwaway certificate for a hostname nobody outside this machine resolves. A REAL DEPLOYMENT ON A REAL DOMAIN MUST SET IT, with includeSubDomains, and this line must not travel with it -- docs/urls-and-tls.md and docs/pitfalls.md both record that as a named gap.
